title: CareCloud (CCLD): The Boring Billing Company That Quietly Became an AI-and-M&A Compounder
content_html:
by Philipp Haas – investresearch.net

Let me start with a scene most of you will recognize.

You go to the doctor as a private patient. A few weeks later a bill lands in your mailbox — but it isn’t from the doctor. It’s from some company you’ve never heard of, with a name you can’t pronounce, and it wants its money. What happened in between? The physician doesn’t want to spend his afternoons chasing invoices, checking insurance codes, and arguing with payers. So he hands the entire billing machinery to a specialist and gets on with treating patients.

That specialist is exactly the kind of business CareCloud (Nasdaq: CCLD) runs — and here I want to correct a small but important misunderstanding, because I had it in my own head at first too. CareCloud is not buying the debt and collecting it like a factoring house. That’s a different, uglier business. What CareCloud does is run the revenue cycle for the provider: it codes the visit, files the claim with the insurer, chases the denials, reconciles the payments, and bills the patient for the remainder. It gets paid a percentage of what it successfully collects. So its interests are aligned with the doctor — the more CareCloud collects, the more CareCloud earns. It never takes the credit risk of owning the receivable. That distinction matters, because it turns what sounds like a grubby collections agency into a sticky, recurring, high-retention software-and-services business.

And that is the whole investment case in one sentence: an unloved US micro-cap that has spent a decade rolling up sleepy little billing shops, bolting its own cloud software on top, and — as of the last eighteen months — quietly wiring artificial intelligence through the entire stack. The market still prices it like a tired healthcare-services roll-up. I think it’s turning into something closer to a vertical SaaS platform. That gap is the opportunity.

At the current price of around $2.54 (Nasdaq close, 5 August 2026 — and note, they report Q2 this morning, more on that later), on my numbers I get to a fair P/E of 22 and a potential return of roughly 34% per year. For a US-listed name, that is a lot of upside, which is why I’ve built a starter position in the Haas Invest4 Innovation Fund.

Let me walk you through how I get there.

1. Product, Business Model, Brand and Moat

What does the company actually do? CareCloud sits at the plumbing layer of US healthcare. Its bread and butter is technology-enabled revenue cycle management (RCM) — the billing engine I described above — sold to everyone from a two-doctor family practice up to hospitals and health systems. On top of that core, it sells a suite of proprietary, cloud-based products: electronic health records, practice-management software, patient-experience tools, analytics, and increasingly a family of AI agents branded stratusAI. Since the 2025 acquisition of Medsphere it also plays in the inpatient software market, including a Black Book–ranked emergency-department information system, which meaningfully widened the pond it can fish in.

How do they make money? Two ways, and they reinforce each other. First, the RCM engine earns a slice of collections — recurring, usage-linked, and remarkably sticky, because once a practice’s cash flow runs through your pipes, ripping you out is a nightmare nobody volunteers for. Second, the software modules are cross-sold into that same installed base of 45,000-plus providers. The genius of the model is the cross-sell: land a small practice through a cheap billing contract, then upsell EHR, analytics, and now AI. That’s textbook vertical-SaaS land-and-expand, dressed up as a services company.

Brand and scale. Nobody outside US healthcare IT has heard of CareCloud, and that’s fine — this is a B2B infrastructure brand, not a consumer one. What matters is the trajectory: revenue has grown from roughly $23 million in 2015 to an expected ~$130 million in 2026, through more than twenty acquisitions, while the reputation among mid-market providers has quietly hardened into “the affordable, tech-forward alternative to the incumbents.” That’s a respectable brand within its niche, and it’s growing.

Moat. Here’s where I temper my enthusiasm honestly. The moat is real but narrow. The stickiness comes from switching costs — mission-critical, cash-flow-linked workflows that providers dread migrating — plus the accumulating data advantage as AI learns across 45,000 providers’ worth of claims. That’s genuine. But CareCloud is not the only roll-up in this space, the underlying RCM service is somewhat commoditized, and a determined larger competitor with deeper pockets could compress margins. So: a moat built on switching costs and integration friction, deepening as AI compounds, but not a fortress. Call it a two-metre wall that’s slowly getting taller.

2. The Market

The US healthcare revenue-cycle and health-IT market is exactly the kind of pond I like: enormous, structurally growing, deeply fragmented, and stubbornly non-cyclical.

  • Big and growing. Americans keep getting sick, getting older, and generating ever-more-complex insurance paperwork. Billing complexity is a feature of the US system, not a bug that’s going away. Every layer of regulation, coding change, and payer friction is demand for someone like CareCloud.

  • Fragmented — which is the point. There are thousands of tiny regional billing shops still running on ageing software and human labour. That fragmentation is the raw material for CareCloud’s whole strategy: buy them cheap, modernise them, plug in AI. The acquisition runway here is measured in years, not quarters.

  • Non-cyclical. Healthcare demand doesn’t collapse in a recession. People delay buying a car; they don’t delay chemotherapy. Revenue tied to claims volume is about as recession-resistant as revenue gets.

  • Political risk — the honest caveat. This is the one soft spot. Reimbursement policy, Medicare and Medicaid rules, and any structural reform of US healthcare financing all wash through this sector. A big enough change to how providers get paid would ripple into how much CareCloud collects on their behalf. It’s not a reason to stay away, but it’s a live variable I keep on the dashboard.

Net-net: a large, growing, defensive market with a decade-long consolidation opportunity, carrying a manageable dose of regulatory risk.

3. Culture and Management

This is a founder-led business, and long-time readers know how much weight I put on that.

The company was built by Mahmud Haq, who remains Executive Chairman — the classic long-horizon founder who has steered CareCloud through a genuinely turbulent decade rather than cashing out at the first bump. Day-to-day is now run by CEO Stephen Snyder, with A. Hadi Chaudhry — himself a former CEO — shifted into Chief Strategy Officer, which tells you the bench has depth and continuity rather than revolving-door churn. Norman Roth holds the CFO seat on an interim basis, the one org-chart line I’d like to see made permanent.

What I like about the culture: the capital discipline is real and repeatable. The acquisitions follow a consistent playbook — asset purchases, priced at roughly one times revenue or less, structured to be non-dilutive to common shareholders, and funded from operating cash flow. That is exactly how a serial acquirer should behave. They then went further and cleaned up the balance sheet: converting the bulk of the Series A preferred into common (killing over $7 million of annual dividend obligations) and fully redeeming 100% of the Series B preferred in May 2026 via a $50 million bank facility, stripping out another $3.2 million a year. That’s a management team deliberately lowering its cost of capital and simplifying the story for institutional investors. Founder-led, disciplined, thinking in decades — this is my kind of team.

I’ll save the one place where I think management stubbed its toe for the risk section, because it’s the single best explanation for why the stock is cheap.

4. Financials, Margins and Recent Developments

The numbers are where the transformation stops being a story and starts being a fact.

Full-year 2025 (the pivot year):

  • Revenue: $120.5 million, up from $110.8 million in 2024 (~9% growth)

  • GAAP net income: $10.8 million, up more than 37% year over year

  • GAAP EPS: $0.10 — the first full-year positive GAAP EPS since the 2014 IPO. Read that twice. After a decade in the wilderness, this business crossed into sustainable profitability.

  • Adjusted EBITDA: $27.5 million, a 23% margin, up around 14–15%

  • Operating cash flow: $28.6 million (+38%); non-GAAP free cash flow: $20.5 million (+55%)

Margins, in the language I care about: a ~23% adjusted EBITDA margin, a net margin in the high-single digits (~7.9%), and — the number that really makes me sit up — a return on equity above 24%. For a company still viewed as a beaten-down services roll-up, a mid-twenties ROE is not what you’d expect. That’s the fingerprint of a capital-light, cross-selling model starting to hit its stride.

Q1 2026 kept the momentum: revenue $31.3 million, up 13% year over year, GAAP net income positive, EPS $0.05. The 13% top-line print is running ahead of the full-year guide, though a chunk is acquisition-fed.

2026 guidance: revenue of $128–132 million, adjusted EBITDA of $29–31 million, and — the headline — GAAP EPS of $0.20–$0.23, which more than doubles the 2025 result. That guided revenue range implies roughly 6–10% growth, which lines up almost exactly with the “7–10%” I had penciled in. The EPS doubling is the part the market seems to be sleeping on.

One under-appreciated detail from the calls: CareCloud grew revenue in 2025 while reducing headcount, explicitly crediting AI-driven automation. That is operating leverage arriving in real time, and it’s why I believe the margin trajectory has further to run.

5. Valuation: The Fair-P/E View

Here’s my framework, the same fair-P/E (faires KGV) approach I apply to everything.

The trailing multiple looks unremarkable at first glance — around 22x on the trailing $0.10 of GAAP EPS. So on the rear-view mirror, the stock looks roughly fairly valued, not cheap. But the rear-view mirror is the wrong instrument here, because earnings are inflecting hard.

I anchor on a fair P/E of 22 for this business. Why 22 and not more? Because I respect the checkered history — the revenue declines earlier this decade, the preferred-dividend arrears, the still-narrow moat all argue for discipline rather than a rich SaaS multiple. And why not less? Because a 45,000-provider installed base, 20%+ ROE, high-20s% EBITDA margins, real free cash flow, and an AI-plus-M&A growth engine deserve better than the low-teens multiple the market slaps on tired healthcare services. Twenty-two is my honest midpoint — the number that neither forgives the past nor ignores the transformation.

Now apply it forward. On 2026 guidance the stock trades at roughly 11–13x GAAP earnings, and on an adjusted-earnings basis the forward multiple slips toward single digits — which is the “single-digit P/E next year” thesis, correctly stated. If EPS doubles into the low-$0.20s this year and keeps compounding into the high-$0.20s over the following two years on the back of cross-sell, AI automation, and disciplined bolt-ons, then a 22x fair multiple on that forward earnings power points to a share price in the neighbourhood of $6 on a roughly three-year horizon.

Run that through the model and it spits out an annualised return of about 34%. The return here isn’t coming from multiple expansion — I’m assuming the multiple stays at fair value. It’s coming almost entirely from earnings growth, which is exactly the kind of return I trust most, because it doesn’t require the market to fall in love, only for the company to keep executing.

6. Risks — Why Is It This Cheap?

If it’s this good, why is it trading at $2.54 and not $6? Fair question. A stock is rarely cheap by accident, and CareCloud gives you several honest reasons.

The checkered past. This is the big one. Revenue actually declined across the earlier part of this decade — from roughly $140 million to $111 million by 2024 — as large health-system clients migrated off a legacy platform CareCloud had acquired. The company only just clawed back to full-year GAAP profitability in 2025. Investors who got burned on the way down are, understandably, slow to re-rate on the way back up. Memory is the most powerful discount mechanism in markets.

The aircraft. Here’s management’s stubbed toe. In among the sensible, one-times-revenue acquisitions, CareCloud set up a subsidiary to purchase an aircraft — justified as a way to visit current and prospective clients. Roth Capital’s analyst put it bluntly: it “doesn’t help,” and it raises fair questions about capital-allocation discipline and whether the acquisition machine is obscuring softer underlying organic growth. I don’t love it either. It’s a small dollar amount, but it’s a signal, and signals matter for a management team asking the market to trust its judgment. I’m watching it.

Serial-acquirer risk. Roll-ups live and die on integration. Buy enough companies and eventually you overpay, or you fail to integrate one cleanly, or the reported growth flatters over organic weakness. The discipline has been excellent so far; the risk is that it doesn’t stay that way.

Micro-cap reality. At a market cap around $100 million, this is small, thinly traded, and volatile. There’s a $60 million ATM equity facility on the shelf — though, to management’s credit, they’ve committed to only issuing shares at or above $5.00, which protects existing holders from dilution at today’s depressed price. Analyst price targets are all over the map, from the low-$2s to $8, and the consensus rating sits at Hold. This is a stock you size as a starter position, not a core holding — which is exactly what I’ve done.

The opportunity exists because of these warts, not in spite of them. The market is pricing the turbulent past and the aircraft misstep, and largely ignoring the doubling earnings and the AI optionality.

7. Latest News and Earnings

The timing here is almost too neat: CareCloud reports Q2 2026 this morning, 6 August 2026, before the open, with the call at 8:30 a.m. Eastern. Consensus is looking for roughly $0.07 of EPS on about $31.9 million of revenue. Given the last few quarters beat on the top line, and given the visible operating leverage from AI automation, this is the print I want to see confirm the thesis. As always, I care less about the headline number than about three things on the call: organic-versus-acquired growth, adjusted-EBITDA margin direction, and any hard metrics on AI adoption.

The other recent developments that matter:

  • May 2026 — acquired Empower Healthcare & Compliance Partners, an asset purchase funded from operating cash flow, adding compliance and advisory services and — crucially — another recurring revenue stream to cross-sell into the 45,000-provider base.

  • May 2026 — Analyst Day at Nasdaq MarketSite, where management laid out four themes I’ll be holding them to: an AI-first platform, a simplified common-stock capital structure, rising free cash flow, and a disciplined acquisition strategy.

  • April–May 2026 — the capital-structure cleanup: the $50 million Citizens/Provident facility and the full Series B preferred redemption, lowering the cost of capital without diluting common holders.

  • June 2026 — a credit-agreement amendment refining the financing terms.

The through-line of every one of these is the same: simplify the story, lower the cost of capital, feed the AI-and-M&A engine.

8. Conclusion: A Re-Rating Waiting to Happen

Let me bring it home.

Strip away the noise and CareCloud is a profitable, cash-generative, founder-led business in a large, defensive, fragmented market, trading at a low-double-digit forward multiple while its earnings are set to double. The base case doesn’t require heroics — it requires management to keep doing the unglamorous things it’s already doing: collect a cut of the bills, cross-sell software, buy small shops at one-times-revenue, and let AI quietly strip out cost. On my fair-P/E of 22, that base case is worth roughly 34% a year, driven by earnings rather than sentiment.

And then there’s the optionality, which is where this gets genuinely interesting.

The AI case. stratusAI isn’t a slide-deck buzzword here — the desk agent already automates a large share of inbound calls, and the company grew revenue while shrinking headcount. If the market ever decides to look at CareCloud as an AI-enabled healthcare-automation platform rather than a billing services roll-up, the multiple doesn’t stay at 22. Vertical-SaaS and AI platforms trade at multiples this stock can currently only dream of. That re-rating is the free call option you get on top of the earnings-driven base case.

The M&A case. A disciplined acquirer buying assets at one-times-revenue and making them “smarter, faster, more valuable” by layering AI on top is a compounding flywheel. Every acquisition that lands cheaply and integrates cleanly is accretive and strengthens the data moat. Do that twenty more times, and the story writes itself.

So the setup is: a solid, understandable base case with real downside protection from cash flow and a disciplined balance sheet, plus two genuine re-rating catalysts — AI-platform recognition and continued smart M&A — that the current price gives you essentially for free. That asymmetry is precisely why I’ve opened a starter position in the Haas Invest4 Innovation Fund. Not a table-pounding all-in — the checkered past and the micro-cap volatility earn it a small size — but a position I’m happy to build into as management keeps proving the transformation is real.

Boring billing company. Quietly becoming something more. Those are often the best ones.
